The central question is whether rotary position embeddings (RoPE) can reliably encode positional relationships for sequence positions never seen during training — and the answer is, largely, no, but the failure mode is subtle. RoPE encodes position by rotating query and key vectors in 2D subspaces by angles θ_d = position × base^(−2d/D); at training length L_train, the model sees a bounded set of rotation angles, and beyond L_train those angles enter regimes where the dot-product similarity function becomes periodic in ways the model has never learned to interpret. The expert worry that beginners miss is the attention entropy collapse: as extrapolated positions produce increasingly aliased or high-frequency rotation angles, attention logits either spike (concentrating mass on a few tokens) or flatten (diffusing mass uniformly), and both failure modes are catastrophic — the former produces repetition/degeneration, the latter destroys positional selectivity entirely. A second expert concern is the perplexity cliff: perplexity doesn't degrade gracefully as sequence length exceeds L_train; instead it holds roughly flat until a sharp discontinuity — typically around 1.2–2× L_train — after which it diverges nearly vertically, suggesting a phase transition rather than smooth generalization failure. Mitigations like YaRN, ALiBi, and position interpolation (Chen et al., 2023) all attempt to address different facets of this — YaRN rescales frequencies to keep angles in-distribution, ALiBi sidesteps rotation entirely — but each introduces its own tradeoffs in near-context fidelity versus far-context extrapolation.

Shallow layers fail differently from deep layers because shallow attention is primarily local and syntactic: their high-frequency RoPE dimensions (fast-rotating subspaces) are still operating within reasonable angular regimes even past L_train, so shallow heads degrade more gracefully, showing entropy increase but not catastrophic collapse. Deep layers, by contrast, rely on low-frequency RoPE dimensions to encode long-range semantic dependencies — exactly the dimensions that wrap around first — so deep heads experience entropy collapse earliest and most severely, a pattern confirmed in the LM-Infinite probing experiments (Han et al., 2023) which show layer-depth-stratified entropy degradation. The attention sink phenomenon (Xiao et al., "Efficient Streaming LLMs," 2023) is actually amplified at the cliff: when positional signal becomes unreliable, heads default to attending to initial tokens as a low-entropy fallback, which consumes attention budget that would otherwise track meaningful long-range content. The problem is that during training, the ratio of rotation speeds across frequency bands encodes implicit geometric structure: the model learns that a particular angular difference between dimension pair (d=0, d=1) versus (d=62, d=63) carries calibrated relative meaning, and rescaling selectively destroys this inter-band ratio even while keeping individual bands in-distribution. Specifically, YaRN introduces a temperature parameter √s applied uniformly to attention logits to compensate for the altered dot-product magnitude — but this is a global scalar correction for what is actually a dimension-specific distortion, meaning heads that relied on cross-band angular relationships receive a systematically miscalibrated similarity signal. The LongRoPE paper (Ding et al., 2024) identifies this as "non-uniform positional interpolation residual error" and demonstrates that even after YaRN rescaling, certain deep heads exhibit persistent entropy elevation (not collapse, but chronic diffusion) at position ranges 8K–16K on a 32K-extended model — exactly the range where inter-band ratios are most distorted. NTK-aware scaling (bloc97, 2023) is even blunter: it shifts the entire base θ to push all dimensions toward slower rotation uniformly, which avoids the inter-band ratio distortion but at the cost of compressing all relative position signals, causing shallow syntactic heads to lose fine-grained local resolution they previously had. The deeper expert concern is that neither approach has a principled way to know which frequency bands were jointly calibrated during training, because that calibration is implicit in weight matrices — so all current rescaling methods are essentially heuristic corrections applied to the input without access to the learned inter-band dependency structure baked into Q and K projection weights.

The failure signature when Q/K-only fine-tuning is insufficient is specific and diagnostic: perplexity recovers at the sequence level but per-layer coherence breaks down, meaning that when you probe intermediate representations at positions beyond L_train, the residual stream carries positionally inconsistent features — tokens at position 4096 have representation geometry more similar to position 512 than to neighboring position 4095, detectable via centered kernel alignment (CKA) similarity matrices across layers. This happens because the V projections and MLP layers downstream of attention have learned to interpret the output distribution of attention under the original positional encoding regime; when Q/K are retrained to produce different attention patterns at long range, the V-weighted value aggregation feeds altered activation distributions into FFN layers whose weights expect the old distribution, causing a representation mismatch that propagates and compounds through depth. The concrete failure mode observed in ablations from the Llama-2 long-context fine-tuning literature is that models fine-tuned with frozen V and FFN weights show recovered perplexity on continuation tasks but catastrophically fail on tasks requiring cross-position information retrieval (e.g., passkey retrieval beyond 16K), because the FFN layers cannot correctly process the semantically novel attention output patterns even when those patterns are positionally accurate. A second failure signature is attention head role drift: heads that were previously specialized (induction heads, previous-token heads) lose their functional identity after Q/K-only fine-tuning because their learned roles were defined jointly by Q/K weights and the downstream expectation of V and FFN — probing classifiers trained on pre-fine-tuning activations drop from >90% to near-chance accuracy on role identification post-fine-tuning, suggesting the fine-tuning has changed what the heads compute without updating what the network expects them to compute. The correct inference is that long-context adaptation requires at minimum joint fine-tuning of Q, K, and V projections together, and ideally includes FFN layers too — which is why methods like QLoRA-based full-attention fine-tuning consistently outperform attention-only parameter-efficient approaches on retrieval benchmarks despite the additional parameter cost.

Yes, and the signature is both detectable and mechanistically interpretable: in SwiGLU/GeGLU architectures, the gate branch computes σ(xW_gate) which produces a soft binary mask over the up-projection activations, and when attention output distributions drift outside their training regime, the gate activations shift toward saturation — either collapsing toward zero (dead gates) or saturating toward one (open gates) — rather than operating in the intermediate regime where the nonlinearity has meaningful gradient and selectivity. Concretely, during normal in-distribution operation roughly 30–50% of GeGLU gates sit in the active intermediate range (roughly 0.1–0.9 after the sigmoid), but measurements on Llama-2 with sequences extended beyond 4K show that gate activation histograms become bimodal and pushed to extremes, with the fraction of intermediate-range gates dropping below 15% in deep layers — this is directly analogous to dead neuron pathology in ReLU networks but arising from distributional shift rather than gradient failure. The mechanistic reason is that SwiGLU gates were trained to be selective over a specific distribution of attention-weighted value aggregates; when positional encoding failure causes attention to diffuse (high-entropy collapse) or spike (sink collapse), the value aggregates entering the FFN are either overly smoothed superpositions or dominated by sink-token features, both of which are out-of-support inputs that drive gates into saturation. Anthropic's analysis of feature superposition (Elhage et al., 2022) provides a complementary lens: FFN layers in superposition-heavy regimes rely on precise input geometry to route computation to the correct feature subspace, and attention-pattern drift destroys this geometric precision, causing the gate to activate the wrong feature directions — detectable as increased FFN output norm variance and decreased cosine similarity between FFN outputs at equivalent semantic positions across different sequence lengths. A particularly sharp diagnostic is the gate entropy metric — computed as −Σ g_i log g_i over gate activation values within a layer — which tracks FFN selectivity directly; in-distribution inputs produce moderate gate entropy while out-of-distribution attention aggregates produce low gate entropy (saturated, indiscriminate gating), and this metric degrades monotonically with sequence length extension in a way that precedes and predicts perplexity cliff onset by roughly 10–15% additional sequence length, making it a potential early warning signal. The practical implication is that gate saturation statistics offer a cheaper diagnostic than full perplexity evaluation for detecting when a length-extended model has exceeded its reliable operating range — you can instrument a forward pass on a validation sequence, compute layer-wise gate entropy, and flag degradation without needing ground-truth labels or a held-out perplexity calculation.

The feedback loop concept is sound in principle — gate entropy collapse precedes perplexity cliff onset by 10–15% sequence length, giving a real intervention window — but the first fundamental obstacle is causal ambiguity: gate entropy collapse is a symptom of multiple failure modes simultaneously (attention sink formation, positional aliasing, value aggregate smoothing), and a feedback signal that conflates these cannot distinguish whether truncation, position rescaling, or attention pattern surgery is the correct intervention, meaning any single corrective action risks being wrong in ways that accelerate degradation rather than arrest it. Concretely, if gate entropy collapse in layer 16 is driven by attention sink formation rather than positional aliasing, triggering context truncation removes tokens that may be carrying valid semantic content while leaving the sink mechanism intact — the model continues to concentrate attention on initial tokens regardless of truncation, so perplexity may actually worsen post-intervention, a failure mode analogous to treating fever with ice packs while leaving the infection untreated. The second obstacle is inference-time latency: computing layer-wise gate entropy requires aggregating activation statistics across all heads and positions at every forward pass layer, adding O(L × D_ffn) operations per layer that cannot be easily parallelized with the existing KV cache computation pipeline — for a 70B-parameter model at 32K context, this overhead is non-trivial and partially defeats the purpose of efficient long-context inference. The third and deepest obstacle is intervention non-locality: attention patterns at layer N are determined by residual stream content that has been shaped by all layers 1 through N−1, so detecting gate entropy collapse at layer 16 and attempting to correct attention at layer 16 does not undo the corrupted residual stream contributions from layers 1–15 — the correction is downstream of much of the damage, making it causally incomplete in a way that truncation or rescaling applied at the input level would not be. StreamingLLM (Xiao et al., 2023) implicitly acknowledges this by applying its attention sink fix at the positional encoding level rather than attempting mid-forward-pass correction, accepting that any intervention must happen before the forward pass commits to a positional regime. A genuinely causally effective feedback loop would require either (a) multi-pass inference where a diagnostic forward pass informs a corrected second pass — doubling latency — or (b) learned intervention policies trained to map gate entropy signatures to specific corrective actions, which reintroduces the training distribution problem: the policy must generalize to exactly the out-of-distribution regimes where gate entropy is most informative but training signal is most scarce.

The obstacle specific to entropy-conditioned mixing coefficients is training stability: if the gate is conditioned on its own layer's entropy, you introduce a feedback path within the forward pass where the gate modulates the very activations that determine the gate value — this creates implicit fixed-point dynamics that are difficult to train with standard backpropagation and can produce oscillatory or degenerate solutions unless carefully regularized, as seen in early attempts at self-attention with learned temperature parameters. A cleaner architectural solution may be cross-layer entropy propagation where a running statistic of gate entropy is maintained in a separate scalar state updated at each layer and used to modulate residual mixing coefficients downstream — this avoids within-layer feedback loops while still providing causal self-correction, and is structurally analogous to the adaptive computation time (ACT) mechanism (Graves, 2016) but applied to representation quality rather than halting decisions.
